items.evidence: AC#1 exhaustive test passes (oracle 7,462 classes, per-category class and hand counts, every hand matches). Read the test: it asserts zero mismatches, a total of 2,598,960, every rank from 1 to 7,462 seen, and handCategory against the oracle category; the mutation probes make it fail. Holdout: my own brute-force scorer over all 2,598,960 hands. The evaluate order matches it exactly (a bijection with 7,462 classes in the same order), the hand counts per category are 40/624/3744/5108/10200/54912/123552/1098240/1302540, and the class counts are 10/156/156/1277/10/858/858/2860/1277 -> PASS.

The worked-examples test passes and asserts all 16 ranks, the 18 category boundaries, HAND_RANK_COUNT and HAND_CATEGORIES order. Holdout: handCategory is called for every rank 1..7462 without error, and the categories match my independent scorer for every hand -> PASS.

AC#2 passes: wheel is 5854, below the 6-high straight and above the best trips; steel wheel is 7453; Q-K-A-2-3 is high-card; Ac 2d 3h 4s 5c 6d 9h is 5855. Holdout: Ac 2c 3c 4c 5c 6d 7d gives 7453 (the straight flush beats the 7-high straight), and Qc Kd Ah 2s 3c 4d 9h is high-card -> PASS.

AC#3 passes for cases (a) to (g). Each case is checked against the listed rank/hand, the max evaluate over its 21 subsets, and the oracle best. Holdout: 12 tricky 7-card hands (7-card SF, two trips, three pairs, quads+trips, wheel with pairs, etc.) equal my own best-of-21 -> PASS.

The property test passes (20,000 seven-card and 5,000 six-card runs, oracle and self-subset max, shuffled order). Holdout: 300,000 seeded random hands (two thirds 7-card, one third 6-card) equal my own brute-force best-of-subsets mapped to dense rank, and the reversed card order gives the same rank -> 0 mismatches.

AC#4 passes: K-K-A-9-4 beats K-K-Q-9-4 (1/-1, both one-pair), the 7-card As kicker wins, and the second kicker decides. Holdout: the exhaustive order equivalence covers every kicker comparison. Note: the AC#4 examples do not involve the lowest kicker, so the 'ignore lowest kicker' probe is caught only by AC#1 and the property tests.

AC#5 example test and the suit-relabelling property (5,000 runs for 5 and for 7 cards) pass. Holdout: the exhaustive check confirms that same-class hands of any suits always give the same rank -> PASS.

Unit test passes with exact RangeError messages. Holdout: lengths 4/8/100 give the exact messages; 52, -1, 1.5, NaN, Infinity, the string '5', undefined, 53 and 1e9 in the first and last positions all give 'Invalid card: <v>'; a duplicate 2c in the 7th position gives 'Duplicate card: 2c'; after errors the next call is clean (rank 1); handCategory 0/-1/7463/2.5/NaN/Infinity give exact messages; compareHands -1/0/1 -> PASS.

Unit test passes. Holdout: parseCard rejects 'as','10s','Ax','','AS','A','Asx','1c','tc','Xs',' 2c' with exact messages; parseCards handles newlines/tabs/runs of whitespace and '   ' -> []; Tc=32, Ac=48, formatCard(0)='2c', formatCard 52/-1 and makeCard(13,0)/(0,NaN) error messages exact -> PASS.

Unit test passes (8,192 flush entries, <5 bits -> 0, straight masks -> 7453..7462, bytes <= 512 KiB, deterministic). Holdout: every flush mask with 5-7 bits equals my brute-force best flush/SF rank; total byteLength <= 524,288 -> PASS.

The perf test passes under npm test with coverage: 2.86M evals/s, build 84.9 ms locally; on CI 1.87M evals/s, build 120.5 ms (floors 1M/s, 500 ms). The test generates hands before timing, warms up, and checks the checksum.

My own exhaustive brute-force check over all 2,598,960 five-card hands gives the same ordering and category counts, 300k random 6/7-card hands match the best of their subsets, and the error messages are exact.
